title: The Story of Rimini: A Poem
description: Hunt's only sustained verse narrative, a romantic tale in rhymed couplets that retells and sympathetically modernises the episode of Paolo and Francesca which Dante set in the second circle of Hell in Inferno V. Where Dante judges the lovers, Hunt dwells on the ill-matched marriage, the slow growth of the attachment and the force of circumstance, treating his subject as human rather than exemplary. Published in 1816 and dedicated to Byron, it was the book that brought the full force of the sectional reviewing of the period down on its author, and it remains the central document of what his enemies called the Cockney school of poetry. Its colloquial diction, its homely domestic detail and its insistence that tenderness could be the matter of a serious poem made it a byword and a battleground in Romantic literary politics.
plot_or_argument: The poem takes from Dante its situation and its persons: Francesca, given in marriage to the lord of Rimini for reasons of policy and not of affection, finds in his brother Paolo the companion her marriage has denied her. Hunt builds his argument not on the crime but on the slow preparation for it, on the dulness of the husband, the loneliness of the wife and the civilities of the court in which their friendship grows. The lovers are at last surprised together and slain, and the poem closes on the fate that Dante assigned to them, the pair still bound in the love that was their condemnation. Throughout, Hunt keeps the reader's sympathy with the actors rather than with the moralist, and treats the famous reading of the tale of Lancelot as the decisive incident in two ordinary lives.
narrative_structure: A single continuous romantic narrative told in order, without frame, allegory or editorial commentary, and organised by the growth of the relationship rather than by incident. Hunt moves slowly through domestic and conversational scenes, so that the poem's action is mostly psychological: the marriage, the acquaintance, the attachment, the discovery and the killing, followed by the brief infernal closing vision taken from Dante. There are no digressive tales within the tale and no competing plots; the machinery of romance is reduced to the few situations needed to make the readers' sympathy inevitable.
principal_characters: Paolo; Francesca; Francesca's husband, the lord of Rimini
literary_form: A narrative or romantic poem in the market for Italian tale-in-verse that Byron's tales had made profitable, but deliberately turned against that fashion's declamation. It is a story poem of ordinary feeling rather than a romance of adventure: no marvels, no contests, no supernatural machinery except the closing Dantean scene. The conventions it works with are those of the colloquial romantic narrative, and its form is that of a plain recital, closer in spirit to a novel reduced to verse than to the epics its reviewers expected of heroic couplets.
meter_and_prosody: Heroic couplets: rhymed pairs of decasyllabic iambic lines, the ordinary English verse of narrative and of polite speech since Pope, and here used with a studied ease and a run-on syntax that many contemporary reviewers thought a violation of the form. Hunt's couplets are continually enjambed, their diction familiar and their imagery domestic, so that the closed mechanical pair becomes the vehicle of a flowing uncourtly narrative voice. The prosody was the poem's most contested feature: its defenders heard naturalness, its attackers heard the absence of verse at all.
historical_context: The poem appeared in the first peace years, when Hunt had just left prison for the sedition committed in the Examiner, when Byron was in exile and when the Edinburgh and Quarterly reviewers were policing the limits of English verse. Its subject belonged to the early nineteenth-century revival of interest in Dante and in Italian story, and its politics belonged to Hunt's liberal London circle, which included Shelley, Keats and Hazlitt. The attacks that followed it in the Edinburgh and Quarterlies, personal as much as literary, were part of the same campaign that degraded Hunt's verse as a Cockney product and made his nose as famous as his poem.
literary_significance: The Story of Rimini is the fullest statement of Hunt's belief that poetry should be written in the language of felt experience and that a subject once judged damnable might be rendered entirely in terms of human tenderness. It gave the Romantic period its clearest instance of criticism as personal and sectional war, and it helped define the party lines of Regency verse, with the Lakers, the Edinburgh reviewers and the Cockney school each defining themselves against the others. Later readers have valued it as a link between Byron's Italian tales and the sensual narrative impulse of Keats, and as proof that Hunt's theory of familiar verse could carry a subject of real weight.
attribution_notes: The poem is undisputedly Hunt's and appeared with his name on its title page; no part of it has been claimed for another hand and no serious question of apocryphality attaches to it. Complications are bibliographical rather than attributive: the volume was reissued in revised form, later editions were printed for other publishers, and the text is therefore not identical across its first issues. Its dedication to Byron is on the face of the 1816 volume and has been taken as evidence of the friendship the two poets later fell out over, but it raises no question about who wrote the poem.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1816 as The Story of Rimini: A Poem, printed by T. Davison, Whitefriars, for John Murray, London, with W. Blackwood, Edinburgh, and Cumming, Dublin, and dedicated to Lord Byron. Copy in the Hathi Trust catalogue records the issue printed by T. Davison for J. Murray and W. Blackwood, and a second edition appeared in 1817, with further issues in 1819 printed by Bensley and Son for Taylor and Hessey, the London firm most identified with Hunt. It was subsequently folded into collections of Hunt's verse and has been reprinted in scholarly selections of his work.

title: The Indicator
description: A weekly literary journal founded, edited and very largely written by Leigh Hunt, issued in London by Joseph Appleyard from 1819 and continued through 1820 and into 1821; its essays were also collected in a two-volume issue dated 1820 to 1821. It was Hunt's attempt to carry the manner of the Examiner into a sheet devoted to poems, tales and short critical essays, and it became one of the founding documents of the familiar Romantic periodical style. Its pages mix definitions of poetry, notices of contemporary verse, reworkings of older stories and sketches of literary character, all in a voice that treats reading as a form of friendship. The Indicator, with The Companion of 1828, is the practical demonstration of the prose Hunt theorised.
plot_or_argument: As a periodical the paper has no argument, but its recurring proposition is that good writing is a kind of conversation and that verse and prose alike should be judged by their humanity and their ease. Numbers carry short essays on poetry and on the poets Hunt admired, reprints and redressings of Italian and English tales, notices of current books and papers of general literary instruction, together with original verse. Its practical polemic is against the hierarchical and personal manner of the great reviews: it proposes instead a criticism of sympathy, addressed to an ordinary reader who buys a penny sheet rather than a quarterly.
narrative_structure: Discontinuous and miscellany-based: a weekly sequence of short numbers, each containing several self-contained pieces, with no plot and no sustained argument across issues. The organising principle is the persona of the editor, who moves between quotation, exegesis, criticism and remonstrance within a single number. Bound runs therefore read as volumes of essays rather than as a serial narrative, and the paper's unity is one of voice, of subject-matter and of the weekly rhythm of appearance.
literary_form: A weekly periodical in the tradition of the Spectator papers and of Hunt's own Examiner, and one of the chief vehicles of the Romantic familiar essay. Its constituent forms are the short critical essay, the literary character sketch, the retold tale, the note on a passage of verse and the occasional poem. The paper is a miscellany rather than a review: it carries no political intelligence and no reports of Parliament, and it subordinates book-notice to the essayist's reflection, which is why it is usually classed with Elia and Table Talk rather than with the Edinburgh Review.
meter_and_prosody: Prose throughout, in Hunt's characteristic familiar manner: short sentences, colloquial vocabulary, first-person speculation and an easy alternation of seriousness and play. Verse appears within the prose in the quoted passages and in the contributed poems, and Hunt's own occasional pieces in the paper are regular in metre, mostly simple lyric or epistle. The prose rhythm is deliberately conversational, closer to spoken ease than to the periodic style of eighteenth-century prose, and it was this quality that later essayists identified as Hunt's contribution.
historical_context: The Indicator belongs to the explosion of small cheap periodicals after 1815, when technological and Circulating-library growth made the weekly sheet a livelihood for professional letters, and to the aftermath of the suppression campaigns that had imprisoned Hunt for the Examiner. Its appearance coincides with the height of the Cockney School controversy, and it gave Hunt a steady income from the press and a platform independent of the great reviews that had insulted him. Its contributors and its circle overlapped with Blackwood's and the London literary world of Hazlitt, Shelley and the younger poets, and its career, like his, ended at the point when Hunt left England for Italy in 1821.
literary_significance: The Indicator established the model of the personal literary weekly that later Romantic and Victorian periodical writing followed, and it is the place where Hunt's idea of a criticism of humanity, rather of judgement, was worked out in practice. Through it the familiar essay became a Romantic institution, setting the manner that his contemporaries and successors copied in the cheap serial press, and shaping how the generation that included his own later collectors understood the relation of verse and criticism. It also documents the economics of authorship: a poet of real distinction earning his living by a weekly sheet. As criticism it remains a key source for Hunt's judgements, for his accounts of Shakespear, Dante and his own contemporaries, and for the quarrels of the Cockney school controversy.
attribution_notes: The journal was published under Hunt's editorship and reference sources state that he wrote much or most of its content, though the weekly numbers carry no consistent individual attributions and the usual practices of periodical composition of this kind mean that the assistance of his literary friends and family cannot be excluded. Its separate authorial identity is secure, but the share of its copy that is Hunt's own is a matter of scholarly inference rather than of documentation, and its collected reissues carry his name as author. Nothing in the evidence supports the transfer of any specific number to another hand.
bibliographical_notes: Published in London by Joseph Appleyard, the weekly numbers beginning in 1819 and running into 1821; bibliographies describe the collected issue as two volumes dated 1820 to 1821, and library catalogues record copies with the Appleyard imprint for 1819 and 1822. Later the paper was reissued with The Companion as The Indicator and The Companion: A Miscellany for the Fields and Fireside, 2 volumes, London: Henry Colburn, 1834, and parts of it were reprinted in Essays by Leigh Hunt: The Indicator, The Seer, London: E. Moxon, 1841-42.

title: Lord Byron and Some of His Contemporaries
alternative_titles: Lord Byron and Some of His Contemporaries; with Recollections of the Author's Life, and of His Visit to Italy
description: Hunt's memoir of Byron and record of their years in Italy, published in London in 1828 in two volumes with recollections of his own life and of the southern sojourn of 1821 to 1825. It is at once a defence of Byron's character, an account of the circle at Pisa and Genoa, a piece of autobiographical exposure and, in its long examination of Don Juan, one of the most ambitious critical essays of the decade. The book gave Hunt his most damaging quarrel with the powerful, because it mixed admiration for his dead friend with frank statement of his own opinions on living authors, and because its candour about its own period made it an authority and a scandal in the same breath.
plot_or_argument: The work sets out to vindicate Byron against the calumnies of his publishers and reviewers, to describe the Italy in which he lived and died, and to give an honest account of Hunt's own dealings with him. Its argumentative core is the Examen of Don Juan, a long critical examination that insists on the poem's seriousness and moral intention against the consensus that it was a degradation of Byron's powers. Between these essays come sketches of contemporaries, recollections of the Hunt brothers and of the Examiner years, and narratives of the journey to Italy, of the society of the Pisan circle and of Byron's last plans. The book's purpose, as its title suggests, is to place Byron within a living literature rather than to bury him in anecdote.
narrative_structure: Two volumes arranged as memoir, recollection and critical essay rather than as a continuous narrative: the biographical account of Byron is interrupted by general criticism, by episodes from Hunt's own life and by portraits of other writers, and the Examen of Don Juan forms the largest single block of sustained argument. There is no chronological spine strong enough to hold the whole together; the ordering principle is the sequence of Hunt's memories and his cases. The result is a mixed form, part memoir, part criticism, part apology, in which the recollecting self is as prominent as the subject.
principal_characters: Leigh Hunt; Lord Byron; the Pisan and Genoa circle of 1821-1825; contemporary authors discussed and characterised
literary_form: A prose memoir and work of literary criticism in the Romantic biographical tradition, close to the character-writing of Hazlitt and to the personal memoir, and built around the review-essay. Its constituent genres are biography, autobiography, personal sketch and the long examination of a single poem, and it belongs to the literature of the periodical even where it is not periodical in form, since its criticism is occasional, argumentative and addressed to a subscribing public interested in living reputations.
meter_and_prosody: Prose, in Hunt's familiar manner: open, conversational, digressive and unforced, with the sententious brevity of the essayist alternating with the longer amble of reminiscence. Verse is quoted throughout for evidence, especially from Don Juan, and the critical passages are shaped by the rhythm of spoken argument rather than by periodic art. There is no metrical composition in the work itself; its prosody is that of prose rhythm and of the quoted lines it is written to defend.
historical_context: Published three years after Byron's death and after Hunt's return from Italy, the book enters the crowded field of Byron memoirs produced since 1823, when publishers, relations and friends competed to define the poet's memory against the attacks of the quarterly press. It also belongs to the history of British literary exile in Italy, to the Pisa circle of Shelley, Byron and their acquaintances, and to the campaign of reputation in which Hunt, now dependent on his pen and on subscription, attempted to speak for a generation. Its reception shows how dangerous such candour was: reviewers of the established journals received it as an act of Cockney presumption, and it deepened the quarrels that had already cost Hunt friends.
literary_significance: It is the principal contemporary witness to Byron's last years from inside his circle, and one of the earliest and most substantial critical defences of Don Juan, a claim for the poem's gravity that later readers have largely accepted. As autobiography it is the fullest account Hunt left of the Examiner years, of the imprisonment and of the London literary world that formed Keats and Shelley, and its sketches of contemporaries are still quarried by biographers. As criticism it marks the moment at which the familiar essay of sympathy was turned on the largest Romantic poem of the age, and it is central to the history of how the Romantics judged one another.
attribution_notes: Authorship by Hunt is certain and appears on the title page of the first issue; the work is, however, a mixed compilation in method, resting heavily on his letters, diaries and personal recollection, and its truth as testimony has long been qualified by reviewers who found its self-interest and its errors of fact irrepressible. There is no dispute about by whom it was written, only about how far it can be trusted as evidence, and much of its later history lies in the corrections and rejoinders it provoked from Byron's friends and from the quarterly press.
bibliographical_notes: Published in 1828 in two volumes, London: Henry Colburn, with the full title Lord Byron and Some of His Contemporaries; with Recollections of the Author's Life, and of His Visit to Italy, and described in library and dealer records as the Colburn issue of that year; some bibliographies label the same year's Colburn edition a second edition, which suggests an earlier issue of portions of the text. It has been reprinted in facsimile from the 1828 copy, and its text, with Hunt's later corrections, is the basis of all modern editions of his autobiographical writing.

title: Peter Bell. A Lyrical Ballad
description: A separate burlesque ballad by John Hamilton Reynolds, published in London in 1819 and running through several editions in that year. Reynolds takes up the title and the manner of the Wordsworthian lyrical ballad and turns them against the school they represented, offering a vagrant hero, a homely moral emergency and a mock-solemn narrative voice in the measure that the Lake school had made famous. It belongs to the lively quarrel over Wordsworth's diction carried on by Hunt's circle in the Examiner and the Champion, and it was one of the pieces that gave the young Reynolds a public name before his association with Keats was remembered.
plot_or_argument: The poem follows the external form of its model: a rough and degraded wanderer, Peter Bell, is led through a series of low adventures to the crisis of feeling at which the original affected to reform him. Reynolds keeps the situation and the humble idiom but lets the rhetoric run over, so that the pathetic and the ludicrous occupy the same stanza, and the moral catastrophe is made to appear as the artifact of a method rather than of an experience. The argument of the piece is critical as well as comic: that the tenderness of the school-poetry could be produced at will by its machinery of diction and metre.
narrative_structure: A single short ballad narrative in continuous order, with no frame, no digression and no editorial intrusion except the mock-dedicatory manner of its title page. The movement is that of the lyrical ballad it parodies, an humble hero carried by successive episodes to a moment of change, and its unity is one of imitated form rather than of plot.
principal_characters: Peter Bell, the vagrant hero of the parody
literary_form: Verse burlesque and parody in the form of the lyrical ballad, written to be read against a well-known original by its own title and measure. As a piece of periodical-school polemics it is nearer to the occasional and satirical verse of the Regency press than to the romantic narrative Reynolds afterwards attempted, and its stanza is borrowed rather than invented.
meter_and_prosody: The ballad stanza of the Wordsworthian model, in common measure with simple rhyme, sustained through a short narrative; Reynolds's point is made by exactness of imitation, so that the prosody is deliberately that of the original and the humour arises from its application.
historical_context: The poem appeared in 1819, the year in which the contest between the Lake school and its younger critics was at its fiercest, and was one of the parodies that followed hard upon Wordsworth's own Peter Bell, bibliographical evidence suggesting that Reynolds's version was in print at about the same moment as the original. It was issued by Taylor and Hessey, Hunt's and Keats's publishers, and belongs with Reynolds's pieces in the Examiner and the Champion to the campaign of the Cockney press against what it took to be the assumptions of the established poets.
literary_significance: The piece is the best surviving evidence of Reynolds's own weight in the literary quarrels of 1819, and of the extent to which the lyrical ballad had become a manner that could be worn, mocked and sold. Its bibliographical history, several editions in a single year, shows that parody of the school-poetry was a commercial form as well as a critical one, and its influence on the practice of Hunt's circle can be traced in the verse and criticism of the years that followed.
attribution_notes: There is no doubt of authorship; the poem is entered in the standard bibliographies of Romantic poetry under John Hamilton Reynolds's name and is recorded in library catalogues as a parody of Wordsworth. It must be distinguished from the poem of the same title which it imitates, and the repetition of the title in the book-catalogues of 1819 has occasionally confused the two.
bibliographical_notes: Published in London in 1819 as Peter Bell. A Lyrical Ballad, printed for Taylor and Hessey; the Jackson Bibliography of Romantic Poetry lists the issue and a third edition from the same publisher in the same year, and library records describe copies of the year with the Taylor and Hessey imprint.

title: The Garden of Florence; and Other Poems
alternative_titles: The Garden of Florence and Other Poems
description: Reynolds's most serious collection of verse, and the book in which his Italian narrative manner, learned from Hunt and from Boccaccio, was given its fullest scope. Its title poem, which bibliographers and earlier commentators describe as a pair of tales in verse named collectively The Garden of Florence, develops the kind of Boccaccian story that Keats was treating at the same moment in Isabella, and it stands at the head of a volume that also carries shorter poems and sonnets. Contemporary accounts of Reynolds's work single out his command of the tender and musical lyric, and the volume as a whole is the best evidence that the Cockney interest in Italian story was a shared enterprise of the group rather than Keats's possession alone.
plot_or_argument: Scholarly accounts of Reynolds's Italian verse identify the title poem as his version of the seventh tale of the fourth day of Boccaccio's Decameron, and the earlier memorials of Reynolds describe the chief poems of the collection as taken from Boccaccio. The tale as Reynolds retells it concerns an attachment that family and money forbid, the attempt to confine the woman who is loved, and her passage at last to Florence; the interest of the poem, in the manner the Cockney school had learnt from Boccaccio, is laid on feeling, tenderness and situation rather than on incident or moral judgement. The shorter poems that follow are occasional and lyrical, among them a piece on Devon which one modern account reports as Reynolds's most successful poem, and a sonnet which he had sent to Keats before printing it here.
narrative_structure: A volume, not a single design: the long Florentine narrative occupies the first part of the book and a section of shorter poems follows it, with the title piece itself, according to the older biographical accounts, made up of two poems carried under one collective name. Within the narrative the structure is that of the plain tale in order, without frame or digression, while the minor pieces are discontinuous lyrics, sonnets and sketches whose organising principle is the sensibility of the writer rather than sequence.
principal_characters: The lovers of the Florentine tale; the speakers of the shorter poems and sonnets
literary_form: Romantic narrative verse in the Italian manner of Hunt's circle, joined to a collection of lyrics and sonnets. The form of the title poem is that of the metrical tale, colloquial, unhurried and devoted to situation and feeling rather than to incident, and it deliberately avoids the machinery and declamation of the Byronic narrative; the shorter poems continue the same interest in tenderness, music and homely detail.
meter_and_prosody: The narrative is in regular rhymed English verse of the Hunt school, with an easy decasyllabic movement and a diction chosen for plainness and for closeness to speech; the shorter poems use simple lyric stanzas and the sonnet, and Reynolds is often praised for the purity of his musical effects. There is no attempt at the spikenard of the Lake school or at Byron's variety, and the effect of sameness and softness that reviewers noticed is a property of the metre as much as of the subject.
historical_context: Published in 1821 by John Warren in London, the volume belongs to the last months of the London group around Hunt and to the years in which Keats's Isabella and Reynolds's own Italian tales were written in conscious emulation of one another; Reynolds alludes to Keats in its preface, and the friendship of the school days had by then become a matter of published record. The book also appears at the point when Hunt himself had left England for Italy, so that the Cockney school it represents was already dissolving.
literary_significance: The Garden of Florence is the chief witness to Reynolds's attempt to make the Boccaccian tale a serious form within the Cockney school, and it is the standard evidence for the rivalry and partnership between his verse and Keats's. Its title poem and its shorter pieces show how widely the fashion for Italian story had spread by 1821, and its reception, and the survival of single lyrics from it in later anthologies, is part of the history of how that fashion was remembered and then discounted.
attribution_notes: There is no doubt of Reynolds's authorship; the volume appeared in his own name and is catalogued among his works, and the only complication is that the title piece is described in the older biographical accounts as two poems published collectively under one name. No part of the book has been claimed for another writer, though the shared habits of Hunt's circle make it difficult to isolate what Reynolds owed to Keats and what Keats's contemporaries thought of as a common manner.
bibliographical_notes: First published in London in 1821 as The Garden of Florence; and Other Poems, John Warren, London; the Jackson Bibliography of Romantic Poetry records the issue as London: John Warren, 1821, and library catalogue records confirm the same year and publisher with John Hamilton Reynolds as author.

title: Odes and Addresses to Great People
alternative_titles: Odes and Addresses to Great People, by the Same Authors
description: A joint volume of comic odes and burlesque addresses by John Hamilton Reynolds and Thomas Hood, published in London in 1825 and reissued in a third edition as early as 1826. The book applies to the elevated Romantic ode, and to the public celebrities and wonders of the moment, exactly the kind of deflating treatment that Reynolds had earlier given to Wordsworth's Peter Bell: its pieces are addressed to great people, to machines, to curiosities exhibited for money and to the fashionable sentiments of the day. It was Hood's first book and one of the last of Reynolds's publications that reached a wide readership, and its success was such that it was still being described, in later accounts of Hood, as the joint beginning of a career.
plot_or_argument: The volume has no continuous argument; its case is made piece by piece against the solemnity of the Romantic ode and against the cult of celebrity. Each address takes a grand form and directs it to an unworthy or absurd subject, so that the rhapsodic manner is exposed by being used where it does not belong; several of the pieces continue the parody of Wordsworthian diction and subject, and one at least, an ode on the aeronaut Graham, is recorded as a parody of Peter Bell. Together the odes and addresses make a comic argument about the difference between real and assumed enthusiasm.
narrative_structure: A miscellany of short separate poems arranged as a sequence of odes and addresses, without plot or sustained progression; the unity is that of a single comic method applied repeatedly to different occasions, persons and exhibits. Individual pieces are self-contained, and the volume reads as a joint notebook of effects rather than as a work with an order of development.
principal_characters: The celebrities, wonders and personified abstractions addressed in the separate pieces; the two comic poets' assumed public voices
literary_form: Burlesque and mock-heroic verse of the recurrent kind, in the specific form of the ode and the address. It works within the Pindaric and Wordsworthian ode as Reynolds's earlier Peter Bell had worked within the lyrical ballad, and it belongs to the tradition of verse that lives on the periodical and the show rather than to the serious romantic narrative; the collaborative character of the volume gives it the texture of a double act.
meter_and_prosody: A deliberate imitation of elevated Romantic metres, used for comic ends: stanzas borrowed from the solemn ode and the pathetic ballad, with their diction and inversions preserved and their subjects replaced, together with the lighter anapaestic and songs measure at which Hood in particular excelled. The success of the writing depends on accuracy of mimicry, and the volume is therefore a useful record of the metrical habits of the generation it laughs at.
historical_context: The book appeared in the later 1820s, when the great decade of Romantic experimentation was being consolidated, imitated and sold, and when parody had become a regular part of the periodical press. Reynolds brought to it the experience of the Examiner and Champion and of the Wordsworth parodies of 1819; Hood was a young contributor whose first book it was. Its reissue by Henry Colburn in 1826, and its survival in the bibliographies of both writers, show how quickly it became a recognised production of the metropolitan literary market.
literary_significance: It is the principal record of Reynolds's last years as a published poet and the founding volume of Hood's career, and it is one of the most sustained examples of the Romantic-period burlesque of the ode. As a joint production it documents the collaboration and friendship that shaped much Cockney writing, and as parody it preserves, in comic form, the manners of Wordsworthian and Hunt-style verse for later students of the period.
attribution_notes: The volume is a collaboration between Reynolds and Hood and is catalogued under both names; the individual pieces were not consistently signed, and the exact distribution of the contents between the two writers rests on later testimony and on the separate bibliographies of Hood and Reynolds rather than on the book itself. The third edition of 1826, which appeared with a different publisher, is described as the work of the same authors, so that the collaboration is documented from the first year of publication.
bibliographical_notes: First published in London in 1825 as Odes and Addresses to Great People, Baldwin, Cradock, and Joy, London; the Jackson Bibliography of Romantic Poetry lists a second edition from the same publisher in 1825 and a third edition from Henry Colburn in 1826, and catalogue records describe copies attributed jointly to Thomas Hood and John Hamilton Reynolds.
